summary: An early Telnet option, from 1974, for agreeing how a vertical tab character in output is handled. It follows the same pattern as the related tab and formfeed options from the same author. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This Telnet option lets the data sender and receiver agree how to handle vertical tab characters in output. It defines several ways to process a vertical tab and rules for choosing the responsible party.

subtitle: A Telnet option for negotiating how output vertical tab characters are handled.

tldr.problem: The sender and receiver need to coordinate which side handles vertical tab characters and what the handling should be.
tldr.mechanism: The NAOVTD option negotiates responsibility and a disposition such as delay, replacement with carriage return and line feed, discard or simulation.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines precedence rules: the sender handles vertical tabs if both parties want to, and the receiver does if neither does.

today: RFC 657 is Historic according to the unit metadata. It documents the NAOVTD Telnet option and its vertical-tab negotiation rules.

sections.title: The NAOVTD Option
sections.content:
RFC 657 defines NAOVTD, or Negotiate About Output Vertical Tab Disposition. It lets the sender and receiver negotiate which party handles vertical tab characters in output.

Without negotiation, neither party is required or prohibited from handling them, though the RFC says the receiver may handle vertical tabs primitively.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is for agreeing who handles vertical tabs in output. Without an agreement, the receiver may still handle them in a basic way.

sections.title: Disposition Choices
sections.content:
A value of 0 means the sender proposes to handle vertical tabs. Values 1 through 250 ask the receiver to handle them with a delay, measured in character-times or NUL characters. Value 251 replaces a vertical tab with carriage return and line feed; 252 discards it; 253 simulates it with enough line feeds to reach the next vertical tab stop; 254 waits for a character on the other simplex connection; and 255 asks the other party to handle it without specifying how.

The sender uses DS (code 1) and the receiver uses DR (code 0) in subnegotiation. The parties use the Telnet DO, WILL, DON'T and WON'T commands to negotiate or refuse the option.
sections.plainLanguage: The value selects what happens to a vertical tab: add a delay, replace it with carriage return and line feed, discard it, simulate it with line feeds or leave the choice to the other side.

sections.title: Selecting the Responsible Party
sections.content:
If neither party wants to handle vertical tabs, the receiver must do it. If both want to, the sender handles them, taking the receiver's suggestions into account.

For delay-based handling, the RFC specifies NUL characters immediately after the line-feed character. Either party can disable further negotiation with the appropriate WON'T or DON'T command.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender handles vertical tabs if both sides want to. If neither does, the receiver must handle them.
